prompt.context: Our client is a major international airline with flights to and from the Americas and Europe. The company already operates two daily flights from A to B, offering connections to C. The CEO has hired Bain to evaluate a new route.
prompt.question: Should the client create a new direct route from A to C?

clarifying_info.q: How many flights per day does the client currently operate on the A-B route?
What aircraft does the client use on the A-B route and what is the load factor?
clarifying_info.a: Airbus A320 (165 seats) with an 80% load factor.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of A-B passengers have C as origin or destination?
clarifying_info.a: 15% of passengers on A-B have C as their origin or final destination.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any competition on the A-B or A-C routes?
clarifying_info.a: One competitor flies A-B daily with an A330 (240 seats) at 80% load factor and has a code-share with a domestic airline on B-C. There is currently no airline flying direct A-C.
Both the client and the competitor charge $600 per leg (one way) for A-B or A-C.

clarifying_info.q: What are the aircraft options and their ranges?
clarifying_info.a: A319 (120 seats, max range 4,000 miles); A320 (165 seats, max range 6,000 miles); A330 (240 seats, max range 7,000 miles).

clarifying_info.q: What are the fixed costs per flight?
clarifying_info.a: A319: $41,000/flight; A320: $62,000/flight. Variable costs are marginal.
A to B: 4,800 miles; B to C: 2,350 miles; A to C (direct): approximately 3,800 miles (shown as route 2 on the diagram).
Yes, the market grows with GDP.

exhibits.title: Route Map
exhibits.shows: A diagram of three cities (A, B, C) connected by three route segments labeled 1, 2, and 3 with their respective distances.

framework: Market sizing / demand estimation: use existing A-B passenger data and the 15% C-origin/destination share to estimate conservative direct A-C demand; also capture competitor passengers who connect through B
Competitive landscape: first-mover advantage on A-C; assess whether the sole A-B competitor would enter A-C after our client does; price parity analysis
Cannibalization vs. incremental revenue: opening A-C will reduce A-B load factor from 80% to 68% (15% of passengers diverted); weigh lost A-B revenue against new A-C revenue
Aircraft selection: route 2 (A to C) is 3,800 miles — only A319 (4,000 mi range) and A320/A330 work; A319 (120 seats, $41k fixed cost) is the most cost-efficient choice for the smaller demand
Profitability of each route post-launch: compute revenue and margin for A-B (post-cannibalization) and A-C separately
Qualitative factors: regulatory/government approvals, first-mover brand benefits, growth potential beyond current connecting passengers, network effects

questions.prompt: Estimate the daily one-way demand for the new A-C route using the client's existing A-B data.
questions.guidance: A strong candidate starts with existing indirect flow: 165 seats × 80% load factor = 132 passengers per A-B flight × 2 flights/day = 264 passengers/day one-way. 15% of these have C as origin/destination = ~40 passengers/day. Then add competitor flow: 240 seats × 80% × 15% = ~29 ≈ 30 passengers/day. Conservative total: 40 + 30 = 70 passengers/day. Candidate should note this is conservative — it excludes latent demand from people who currently don't travel because there is no direct route.

math.setup: Client A-B demand with C connection: seats × load factor × pct_C × flights_per_day; Competitor flow: seats × load factor × pct_C × flights_per_day
steps: 264 × 15% = 39.6 ≈ 40 passengers/day with C as origin or destination

questions.prompt: Which aircraft should the client use for the A-C direct route?
questions.guidance: A-C distance is 3,800 miles (Route 2 on diagram). A319 max range is 4,000 miles — just sufficient. A320 and A330 also reach, but A319 has the lowest fixed cost ($41k) and is appropriately sized for ~70 passengers. A330 (7,000 mi range) is oversized and too expensive. Candidate should confirm range feasibility before cost analysis.

math.setup: Compare each aircraft's range vs. 3,800-mile requirement; pick smallest/cheapest that qualifies
steps: A319: 4,000 mi range ≥ 3,800 mi — feasible; fixed cost $41,000
A320: 6,000 mi range — feasible; fixed cost $62,000
A330: 7,000 mi range — feasible; fixed cost not given (assumed higher)
70 passengers < 120 seats on A319 — capacity sufficient
math.answer: A319 is the appropriate choice: range-feasible, lowest fixed cost, adequate capacity for 70 passengers

questions.prompt: Calculate the profitability of the A-B route after the new A-C route launches (post-cannibalization).
questions.guidance: When A-C launches, 15% of A-B passengers divert, reducing load factor from 80% to 68%. Revenue and cost for the A-B route should be recalculated. Margin should still be positive.

math.setup: Post-cannibalization A-B load factor: 80% × (1 - 15%) = 68%; Revenue = 165 × 68% × $600; Cost = $62,000
math.answer: A-B route remains profitable at ~8% margin per flight after cannibalization

questions.prompt: Calculate the profitability of the new A-C direct route.
questions.guidance: Use 70 passengers/day at $600/ticket on an A319 with $41,000 fixed cost. Margin is thin but positive.

math.setup: Revenue = passengers × ticket price; Cost = fixed cost per flight; Margin = (Revenue − Cost) / Revenue
math.answer: A-C route yields ~2.5% margin per flight — thin but positive

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should be considered before recommending the client launch the A-C route?

categories.name: Competitive response
ideas: Competitor may enter A-C once client establishes the route, eroding first-mover advantage
Competitor could retaliate by cutting fares on A-B to recapture share
First-mover brand recognition and frequent-flyer loyalty on A-C could deter entry

categories.name: Demand upside
ideas: Conservative estimate excludes latent demand — travelers who avoid the indirect route today
GDP growth implies market expansion over time
New direct service may stimulate tourism or business travel previously not captured

categories.name: Operational considerations
ideas: Ground handling and crew base requirements at C
Maintenance support for A319 at new destination
Schedule coordination to avoid passenger confusion between A-B and A-C flights

categories.name: Regulatory and legal
ideas: Bilateral air service agreements between the countries of A and C
Foreign ownership and traffic rights regulations
Environmental permits or landing charges at new airports

categories.name: Financial risk
ideas: 2.5% margin is vulnerable to any cost increase or demand shortfall
Fuel price volatility could make the A-C route unprofitable quickly
A trial period with defined success metrics reduces downside risk

recommendation: Launch the A-C direct route, starting with a trial using the A319
The A-B route remains profitable at ~8% margin even after 15% cannibalization, and A-C contributes a positive, though thin, 2.5% margin
Client is first mover on A-C — no competitor currently flies it — providing a window to capture the full market and build loyalty before a rival can respond
risks: Margin on A-C (2.5%) is thin; cost overruns or below-70-pax load would make the route unprofitable
Competitor may launch a competing direct A-C service, eliminating price/convenience advantage
Regulatory approvals for new international route may delay or block launch
next_steps: Run a 6–12 month trial of the A-C route and track actual load factors vs. the 70-pax estimate
Monitor competitor response on both A-B and any A-C entry plans
Evaluate yield management and ancillary revenue options to widen the 2.5% A-C margin
Pursue regulatory approvals and airport operating agreements at C in parallel
